column8: Mon 16 Nov: 3a/3e store, the US bulk price of a fixed promise (99.9%-102.9% of liabilities valued on an AA corporate curve, Aug 2026); an input to row 10, never set beside $1.11 without row 3's change of yardstick.

Mon 16 Nov: 3e store, the yardstick gap behind rows 3 and 20; the 4.98% ten-year zero reproduces on the engine from the repo's Sep 2026 curves (18 closes); HQM includes A-rated bonds, so say about 0.9 points.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a input to row 10; $275,881 (91.5%) reproduces on the engine with a 0.9-point par shift and $301,544 is NUMBERS 3; rough, and Laura is far too small for the bulk market, so a yardstick only.
Mon 16 Nov: 3a/3e store, a regulator's proxy for insurers' buy-out prices (gilts plus 0.3%-0.6%); consultation rates, so say proposed.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a input to row 10; $292,702 and $284,152 reproduce on the engine (par shifts of 0.3 and 0.6 points, in line with Q68-036's $286,970 at 0.5); use $0.97 as the honest like-for-like bulk price.
Mon 16 Nov: store only; insurer prices move several percent with competition and spreads, context for row 10; the LCP figures are trade press, read LCP itself before citing.

Mon 16 Nov: 2.3 and 3a, why an insurer is cheaper: it backs annuities with corporate and private debt, so the promise rests on those loans, which IPS l.11's anybody else's money rules out; pairs with Q2b-022.
Mon 16 Nov: store only; a share of required capital, not of liabilities, so never set 140%-190% beside the 111.4% funded ratio (NUMBERS 8h).
Mon 16 Nov: store only; the scale of the US transfer market, nothing near $500,000; context for 2.3 at most.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a and 3e, the like-for-like answer to dear or cheap; $45,487, $45,456 and the $31 fee gap reproduce from NUMBERS 8h, but in expectation must become at today's forward rates (8h values are forward values, not a forecast), and $1.11 is the 1 Jan 2033 ratio: up front it is about $1.12 ($336,656 against $301,544, NUMBERS 2 and 3), so 15-21 cents above a bulk insurer; add that an annuity is not a permitted holding, so insurers are a yardstick, never an option.

Mon 16 Nov: 2.3 support, the law of one price makes the Treasury curve the honest cost of fixed dates; read only as quoted in Powell's slides (and Powell disputes it), so check the wording in Staff Report 500 or the AER text before quoting.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a, the retail benchmark: buyers paid 4.4%-7.0% above Treasury value for 10- to 15-year term annuities ($1.04-$1.07), never returned; Table 2 read at source; level immediate annuities, so say about.

Mon 16 Nov: 2.3 or 3e, an insurer's price fell below Treasury value in late 2008 because reserve rules let it book less than a dollar per dollar owed; say buyers were in the end paid, so the point is what backs a price, never that cheap buyers lost.

Mon 16 Nov: 2.2 and 3a, retail buyers give up about half a point of yield for the convenience of not building a ladder (Poterba and Solomon's own words); $310,687-$316,955 reproduce on the engine; one date's quotes.
Mon 16 Nov: store only; insurers price off their own asset yields (BBB), supporting row 7; life annuities carry longevity pooling the ten do not need.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a, the market's price of rate-risk management on annuities is about 8 points, never returned; life annuities and full text unread, so never set 8 points against the plan's 11% as like for like, and name what comes back by figure, never most.
Mon 16 Nov: store only; a second market (Canada, 2018 data) where annuity prices are set off corporate yields; adds little beyond rows 7 and 15.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a beside AHA row 5's PRA clause (Q73-025): a US insurer reserves at the average of its worst 30% of scenarios on its own assets' earnings, the extra Treasuries for cash earning nothing; capital sits on top, so one clause.

Mon 16 Nov: store only; the survey's best estimate and worst case are deferred-life (mortality) assumptions, not rate standards, so say insurers mostly reserved at best estimate before VM-22, never that Laura's standard is the 6% kind.

Mon 16 Nov: 3e answer to you over-reserved; the 0.915 factor is Laura's ten's ratio applied to pension liabilities whose durations and curves were not read (US accounting uses AA, HQM includes A), so read the durations first or say if their duration were near ten years; 111.4% matches NUMBERS 8h.
Mon 16 Nov: twin of H7-008 (lottery prizes priced by Treasuries on the day); carry the Pennsylvania Code's competitive-bid wording there as its source.
Mon 16 Nov: the use (the extra Treasuries are the price of coupon bonds where a lottery holds zeros) is Q17-010's; name the practice, never STRIPS as anything Laura could hold.
Mon 16 Nov: 2.3 or 3d, one fixed payment priced three ways by who stands behind it (court record, 2003): a vivid single case for the ladder of prices; one case, payment rights only.
Mon 16 Nov: row 23 restated in yields; the 5.6% and 86 cents reproduce (about 7.6 years at 3.6%); fold into row 23.

Mon 16 Nov: store only; the two points also price illiquidity, assignment costs and the buyer's margin, not ownership alone; drop can sell at market (the plan holds to maturity, IPS l.17) and say held for her (UCC 8-503); the 2002 quote read only in the opinion.
Mon 16 Nov: store only, the seller's end of the ladder of prices (54%-60% of federal-rate value, California 2000-03); rates sought, not approved.

Mon 16 Nov: 3e, names the extra Treasuries self-insurance with a shadow price ($31 of fees at forwards plus a lower range, NUMBERS 4 and 8h); adds the theory to H5-032; cite Ehrlich and Becker only, never the 1985 paper without its authors.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a/3b, a premium that refunds itself in proportion to rates, against an insurer's markup paid away; $45,456, $43,469, $18,053, $14,361 and $0 reproduce from NUMBERS 8h and 8k, but drop the 96% and 40% (window figures are at each window's own rates, $45,456 at forwards, so the ratios are not in NUMBERS) and name each figure's money as AHA row 5 asks; carries Q25-027's figures.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a and 3e, the honest half of you over-reserved: the price falls on the range ($33,150 of floor payout; $95,000-$115,000 against $125,000-$155,000 with no margin, NUMBERS 4), not on her wealth; figures match.

Mon 16 Nov: 3a, both cheaper routes fail IPS l.11 (quotes exact; $22,192 short at 0% matches NUMBERS 2); say first that an annuity is not a permitted holding (6 Oct Wharton email, H5-065), so the insurer route is a yardstick only.
Mon 16 Nov: the explanation row 10 already gives (who keeps the spread); carry its plain sentence there: an insurer is cheaper because it takes risks with the money.
Mon 16 Nov: 2.3 store, above a guaranty cap an annuity is a corporate obligation; extends Q2b-022 by one clause; say above the caps found, never any cap.
